claims.claim: Eventstreams ingest, transform without code and route events; CDC source connectors for Azure SQL, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server on VM capture a snapshot then changes.

Destinations include custom endpoint, eventhouse (direct ingestion or processing before ingestion), lakehouse (Delta) and Activator; Contributor or higher is required for eventhouse, lakehouse and Activator destinations.

concept_html:
An eventstream brings real-time events into Fabric, optionally transforms them, and routes them to destinations, without code. It is Microsoft's recommended path for low-latency, event-driven ingestion (lesson C4-L1).

Sources include Azure Event Hubs, IoT Hub, custom apps, and change data capture (CDC) connectors for Azure SQL Database, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server on a VM. A CDC source first captures a snapshot of the current data, then streams the changes.

Transformations are no-code operators on the stream: filter, manage fields, aggregate over a time window, group by, union, join, expand. You can split one stream into derived streams for different consumers.

Destinations (Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026):

  • Eventhouse, for KQL analysis (lesson C7-L2). Two ingestion modes: direct ingestion, or event processing before ingestion when you apply transformations in the eventstream first.
  • Lakehouse. Events are converted to Delta Lake format and written to lakehouse tables.
  • Activator, to trigger actions on conditions (lesson C7-L3).
  • A custom endpoint, to route events to your own application.

Writing to an eventhouse, lakehouse or Activator destination needs Contributor or higher on the destination's workspace.

Design choices that matter:

  • Filter early. Drop events nobody needs in the eventstream, before they cost storage and query time.
  • Keep the raw stream. Route an unfiltered copy to an eventhouse or lakehouse table as your bronze layer, and derive cleaned streams from it. You cannot replay events you dropped.
  • Decide the event time. Events carry their own timestamp. Use it for windows and analysis, not the time of arrival, which drifts when senders buffer or reconnect.

lines: Destination 1: Eventhouse table telemetry_raw        (direct ingestion, every event)
Destination 2: Activator rule on faults               (alert within seconds)
Destination 3: Lakehouse table bronze.vehicle_faults  (Delta, for Spark models)

exercises.prompt: Write `route(event: dict[str, object]) -> list[str]` modelling the strong design. Every event goes to `"telemetry_raw"`. Events with `event_type == "fault"` also go to `"activator_faults"` and `"bronze.vehicle_faults"`. Events without an `event_type` key go to `"telemetry_raw"` and `"quarantine"`. Return destinations in that order.
exercises.prompt_html: Write route(event: dict[str, object]) -> list[str] modelling the strong design. Every event goes to "telemetry_raw". Events with event_type == "fault" also go to "activator_faults" and "bronze.vehicle_faults". Events without an event_type key go to "telemetry_raw" and "quarantine". Return destinations in that order.
exercises.solution:
def route(event: dict[str, object]) -> list[str]:
    """Destinations for one telemetry event. Every event is kept raw.

    Args:
        event: Parsed event.

    Returns:
        Destination names in routing order.
    """
    destinations = ["telemetry_raw"]
    if "event_type" not in event:
        destinations.append("quarantine")
    elif event["event_type"] == "fault":
        destinations += ["activator_faults", "bronze.vehicle_faults"]
    return destinations

title: Eventstream, events in, routed out
why_html: A fleet team filtered its eventstream to keep only engine-fault events and wrote those to an eventhouse. Three months later, engineers needed the normal readings before each fault to build a failure model. They had never been stored. Keeping the raw stream in a cheap table, and deriving the fault stream from it, would have preserved the history the model needed.
